topics.title: Span<T>, Memory<T> & Allocation-Aware APIs
topics.summary: Work with contiguous memory safely while avoiding unnecessary allocations/copies on measured hot paths.

concepts.name: Span<T>
concepts.explanation: Span<T> is a stack-only ref struct view over contiguous memory. Slicing a span creates another view instead of copying the underlying data.

concepts.name: Memory<T>
concepts.explanation: Memory<T> is not stack-only and can cross async boundaries or be stored on the heap; its Span property exposes synchronous span access.

concepts.name: Measure first
concepts.explanation: Allocation reduction is valuable in hot paths, but ref-heavy APIs increase complexity. Profile before replacing simple string/array code with low-level memory abstractions.

topics.challenge: Write a method accepting ReadOnlySpan<char> and slice it at least once without creating a substring for every part.
topics.hint: Use range slicing such as span[..index] and span[(index + 1)..].

references.title: Microsoft Learn — Reduce allocations and copies

topics.title: Expression Trees & Code-as-Data
topics.summary: Represent lambda expressions as inspectable expression trees for query providers, rules engines, mapping, and dynamic composition.

concepts.name: Delegate versus tree
concepts.explanation: Func<T,...> is executable behavior. Expression<Func<T,...>> is a data structure describing the expression and can later be compiled or translated.

concepts.name: Tree nodes
concepts.explanation: Expression trees contain nodes such as parameters, constants, member access, calls, and binary operations. Libraries can inspect these to build SQL or other representations.

concepts.name: Limits
concepts.explanation: Not every C# construct can appear in an expression tree, and providers support different subsets. Keep translated expressions within the target provider capabilities.

topics.challenge: Create an Expression<Func<...>>, inspect at least one property of its Body, then compile and invoke it.
topics.hint: The important distinction is that the expression variable stores a tree before Compile turns it into executable delegate behavior.

topics.title: Async Streams & IAsyncEnumerable<T>
topics.summary: Produce and consume values over time with async iterators without waiting for an entire asynchronous collection to materialize.

concepts.name: Async iterator
concepts.explanation: An async iterator returns IAsyncEnumerable<T>, uses yield return, and can await between produced values.

concepts.name: await foreach
concepts.explanation: Consumers enumerate asynchronous streams with await foreach, receiving values as they become available.

concepts.name: Cancellation
concepts.explanation: [EnumeratorCancellation] can connect a cancellation token parameter with WithCancellation/consumer cancellation semantics in custom iterators.

topics.challenge: Write an async iterator that awaits between yielded values and consume it with await foreach.
topics.hint: The method return type is IAsyncEnumerable<T>; inside it you can combine await and yield return.

topics.title: Variance, Advanced Generic Constraints & Generic Algorithms
topics.summary: Understand covariance/contravariance and express generic algorithms over precise capabilities without unsafe casts.

concepts.name: Covariance
concepts.explanation: out type parameters permit a generic interface/delegate to produce a more derived type where a base type is expected, such as IEnumerable<string> used as IEnumerable<object>.

concepts.name: Contravariance
concepts.explanation: in type parameters permit consumers of a base type to stand in for consumers of a derived type in supported generic interfaces/delegates.

concepts.name: Constraints as capabilities
concepts.explanation: Multiple constraints can require interfaces, constructors, nullability/value/reference semantics, or static abstract members so algorithms remain type-safe.

topics.challenge: Demonstrate one valid generic variance assignment and write a generic method with at least two constraints.
topics.hint: Remember the direction: producers are commonly covariant (out), consumers are commonly contravariant (in).

references.title: Microsoft Learn — Generic types and methods

topics.title: Unsafe, Interop, GC & Performance Engineering Capstone
topics.summary: Recognize when advanced runtime techniques are justified and how to measure allocations, pinning, native boundaries, unsafe code, and garbage-collection behavior.

concepts.name: Unsafe and interop
concepts.explanation: unsafe code and pointers can bypass some runtime safety for specialized memory/native interop scenarios. P/Invoke and source-generated interop cross managed/native boundaries.

concepts.name: GC pressure
concepts.explanation: Allocation rate, object lifetime, large objects, pinning, finalization, and retained references influence garbage-collector work. Optimize from profiler evidence, not folklore.

concepts.name: Engineering discipline
concepts.explanation: Advanced optimization requires a baseline, a reproducible benchmark/profile, one controlled change, and verification that correctness and maintainability remain acceptable.

topics.challenge: Write a small unsafe pointer example or, if you prefer safe code, rewrite the same operation with Span<T> and explain why you would choose one approach.
topics.hint: Unsafe code should be an explicit tool for measured/native requirements, not a badge of seniority. A safe Span<T> solution is often the better answer.
